title: 800 visits, 1 donation, and a message that made my day — SpriteMaster update
author: Dream_Ep
selftext:
A few days ago I posted here about SpriteMaster — a free browser-based tool to turn AI-generated videos into game-ready sprite sheets.

Here's what happened since launch:

* 800+ visits
* A ton of feedback (seriously, you guys don't hold back and I love it)
* My first donation ever

That last one hit different. The message that came with it was in French and roughly translates to:  "A big thank you. At the beginning of a development, you start from zero. With this, you can truly let creativity express itself and evolve the project. Excellent work!"

Someone out there found enough value in what I built to actually support it. That's a first for me and it means a lot!

What I've shipped since launch (based on YOUR feedback):

* GIF video support — You can now process animated GIFs directly, not just MP4/WebM
* 320px resize option — For those of you making Discord stickers or working at smaller resolutions
* Increased max size to 1024px — More flexibility for higher-res sprites
* Per-sheet resize in the Sheet Manager
* Improved merge UX and a new flip section
* General tool polish across the board

Most of these came directly from comments and DMs. You asked, I shipped. 

Feedback is still very welcome. If something feels off, if you want a feature, or if you hit a bug — let me know. I'm actively developing this and every suggestion gets considered.

Give it a try: [https://spritemaster.pages.dev/](https://spritemaster.pages.dev/)

Thanks for being such a great community. Back to building (the tool, not my game... I'll get to that eventually).

[\\"volt runner\\" example with 3 animation \(run, dash and death\) - Produced thanks to the AI workflow described in the website](https://preview.redd.it/01oeur4bc1jg1.png?width=1024&format=png&auto=webp&s=00d7367228419660ef1f9894fa0caa218e1badc2)

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
This seams like one of the few useful tools posted here even for non AI related stuff so well done for that.

However I think the problem with things like this is that people have been burnt too many times. Companies or individuals release tools like this and then as soon as it becomes popular they start adding in paid options and restrictions on free use.

That often turns people off things like this because they don't want to get used to using a tool just to have it vanish or become monetised 6 months down the line.

It doesn't help that the website has a very corporate looking style where you are expecting to find the paid subscription tier page either.

If this runs completely locally and is completely free "forever" then why not put it on GitHub or release it as a standalone app?

Whilst having things work in the browser is convenient you're still at the mercy of the tool just vanishing one day.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
Thanks a lot, really appreciate you saying that — and your concerns are completely valid. This bait-and-switch pattern is everywhere and I get the skepticism.

So let me be straightforward:  It won't become paid. No Pro tier, no credits, no "free for 30 days." The tool is free, period. The whole thing runs client-side — your files never leave your browser, there's no server processing anything. My operating cost is literally a $12/year domain. Cloudflare hosts it for free. There's no per-user cost that would ever pressure me into gating features behind a paywall.

On the corporate look — fair point honestly. I'm a solo dev who probably spent too long on the landing page. There's no company behind this, no investors, no team. Just me building something I needed myself. I just wanted to make it the more attractive possible and serious so users can actually be interested to use my tools and make the first step to it!

On it vanishing — since everything runs 100% in your browser (Canvas API, zero server calls), you could technically save the page and run it offline forever. But more practically: when something costs $1/month to run, there's no reason to shut it down. It's not like I'm burning through cloud compute bills.

On open-sourcing — I'm keeping the code private for now, but I'm not ruling it out later. For the moment, the "it could vanish" concern is really addressed by the architecture: no backend means no kill switch.

If you ever want to give feedback or suggest features, there's a GitHub Issues link in the footer — I actually read everything that comes in. And if you find it useful, there's a small "buy me a coffee" link, but that's it — no guilt trips, no pop-ups. :)

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Ok that's good to know. Can I ask how you get hosting for free?

I've got a few web based ideas like this myself but as you are probably aware you're lucky if even 0.1% of users donate when something is free so having such low running costs would help.

Btw the website looks great. It's just that the overall style is similar to so many sites that are trying to sell you a subscription which might turn a few people away. People are often much more skeptical now when something is completely free and closed source unfortunately.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body:
Thanks! The secret is that SpriteMaster is 100% client-side — all the image/video processing happens in your browser using the Canvas API. There's no server doing any work, so there are no per-user compute costs. The site is just static files hosted on Cloudflare Pages (free tier), so my only real cost is the potential domain name at \~$12/year but at the moment I don't even pay the domain since it's a .dev domain haha. Even if the site gets 500K visits a month, it stays within the free tier. That's the beauty of client-side architecture for tools like this !

Fair point on the landing page style , I can see how the polished look might trigger "SaaS subscription incoming" vibes. I'll think about ways to make the free aspect more obvious upfront. If you have any idea how to make the free vibe more obvious but the user want to use it thanks to the nice aspect please tell me all your advice ! :)

The reason it's closed source is mostly about protecting the work that went into it, not about hiding anything shady — your files never leave your browser, which you can verify in the network tab.

If you're building similar web-based tools, I'd definitely recommend the client-side approach. As long as the browser APIs can handle your use case, your hosting costs are essentially zero regardless of traffic.
